text: James Vernon the Younger (15 June 1677 – 17 April 1756) was a British government official, courtier, diplomat, and Whig politician who served in the House of Commons from 1708 to 1710. He served as British envoy to Denmark from 1702 to 1707 and was groom of bedchamber to the Prince of Denmark from 1702 to 1708. He was the eldest son of James Vernon and Mary Buck, daughter of Sir John Buck, 1st Baronet, of Hamby Grange, Lincolnshire; his father was Secretary of State under William III. Vernon was educated at Utrecht in 1690, at Rotterdam from 1690 to 1692, and again at Utrecht from 1696 to 1697. In 1691, he was appointed serjeant of the chandlery and in 1697 became an extra clerk of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council. His first parliamentary attempt was in a by-election in 1698 at Penryn, where he failed. From 1698 to 1700, he was groom of bedchamber to the Duke of Gloucester, from whose illness he contracted the disease that caused the Duke's death, and he recovered over several months. At the 1701 general election, he and his father contested St Mawes but were unsuccessful. From 1701 to 1702, he served as a Commissioner of the privy seal. In May 1702, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. In 1708, he was returned as Whig Member of Parliament for Cricklade. In early 1709, he supported the naturalization of the Palatines, and in 1710 voted for the impeachment of Dr Sacheverell, later expressing disappointment that Whig leaders had made a big deal about ‘a factious preacher much below their notice’. He became a Commissioner for excise in 1710, in compensation for his father's dismissal as teller of the Exchequer; the post, worth £800 a year, made him ineligible to stand in the 1710 general election. Vernon disengaged from politics and served the Tory administration as an official. In 1713, he married Arethusa Boyle, daughter of Charles Boyle, Lord Clifford of Lanesborough, and with whom he had issue, including Francis Vernon, who died in 1783 and was created 1st Earl of Shipbrook (I). When King George I ascended the throne in 1714 and the Whigs were in power, Vernon's Whig background benefited him; he retained his position and was appointed a Clerk of the Privy Council in 1715, a post he held for life. In 1716, he again served as Commissioner of the Privy Seal. He lost his excise post in 1726 due to a disagreement with Walpole, but it was restored in 1728. In 1727, he succeeded his father. Vernon devoted himself to religious and charitable works, including sponsoring the foundation of the colony of Georgia and serving as a trustee for Bray's charity. Though his government duties kept him in London, by 1733 he purchased an estate at Great Thurlow, Suffolk, for £15,000, and later built workhouses for several Suffolk parishes. He died on 15 or 17 April 1756 and was buried at Great Thurlow.
